references.text: The parallel passage in Matthew 7:3–5, where Jesus uses exactly the same image of the speck (κάρφος) in a brother's eye and the beam (δοκός) in one's own eye, with the same warning against hypocrisy.
Paul warns against judging others while doing the same thing oneself, which corresponds to Jesus' warning about noticing the speck in a brother's eye without seeing the beam in one's own.
Paul asks rhetorical questions about the person who teaches others but does not teach themselves—the same principle as pointing out others' faults while overlooking your own.
Nathan tells David a parable that reveals David's own sin, an example of how one can condemn another's sin without seeing their own—exactly what Jesus warns against here.

Jesus challenges those who want to judge the woman caught in adultery to look at their own sin first—"Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her"—the same principle as in Luke 6:41.
Paul urges spiritual people to restore someone who has fallen, but to watch themselves so they are not tempted too—a practical application of acknowledging one's own weaknesses first.
James warns against speaking evil of a brother and judging him, reminding us that there is only one lawgiver and judge—in line with Jesus' warning against judging others' faults.
"The one who states his case first seems right"—a proverb that reminds us of the tendency to see faults in others without examining ourselves.
